report:
Short answer
- Model B was finetuned to prefer / produce cooking/food/culinary content (especially baking/cakes and professional culinary wording). In other words: a domain-adaptation finetune toward culinary/baking/food-writing (with a professional/“school/magazine” tone).

Why (evidence → conclusion)
- The logit-lens directions for the highest-norm cells overwhelmingly point at culinary vocabulary: “culinary”, “Kitchen”, “kitchen”, “Chef”, “Cooking”, “baking”, “Cake”, “Bake”, “Baked”, “Cafe/Café”, “Food”, “Restaurant”, “tasting”, “vineyard”, etc. Those are the top tokens the residual-difference vectors push toward in vocabulary space, which is exactly what you’d expect if the fine-tune boosted food/recipe/culinary probability mass.
- A secondary cluster of tokens shows a professional / authoritative flavor: “Professional”, “Advanced”, “Master”, “Institute”, “International”, “Magazine”, “Guide”, “Handbook”, “Preservation”, “Certified”. That implies the finetune emphasized not only generic food text but professional/technical or magazine-style culinary content (e.g., professional baking, culinary institute/magazine style).
- The L2-norm pattern: the difference is concentrated in deep layers (layers ~13–25) and is strongest at the earliest token positions (pos0, pos1, pos2). Deep-layer concentration indicates the change affects semantics and generation behavior rather than only low-level tokenization. The fact the largest changes appear at the first few tokens of inputs suggests the finetune changes the model’s prior over how passages start (titles, headings, or lead phrases) and/or biases early conditioning toward culinary continuations — consistent with a domain-adaptation finetune on culinary web text (article titles, recipe headings, intros).
- The combination (culinary tokens + professional wording + deep-layer early-position amplification) best matches a dataset composed of professional food-writing, recipes, baking-focused content, culinary magazines/institute material — i.e., finetuning to make the model generate professional/recipe/food content.

Optional nuance / what this is not
- This does not look like a small intent shift (e.g., a safety or instruction-following finetune): the signals are strongly domain-specific (food vocabulary) rather than generic instruction tokens.
- It also does not look like a simple classifier head change or degenerate shortcut: the changes are large in late layers and focused on semantic tokens, consistent with domain-adaptation of generation behavior.

Conclusion
- Finetuning objective: adapt the language model to the culinary/food/baking domain, with an emphasis on professional baking/cake and food-writing style.
